One commenter first expected 'a cross-cloud Terraform' and disliked the idea of DBs being spun up on EKS/GKE rather than managed services. After reading the design doc, they called it 'Very clever': cloud-agnostic custom resources with cloud-specific controllers. Their caveat: 'You have to set up your own k8s manually (there's no way to bootstrap).'

Compared to the AWS Service Operator: Crossplane's model resembles Kubernetes Persistent Volumes, where an abstract class is fulfilled by concrete per-cloud implementations. Using AWS Operator APIs directly in a Helm chart ties the app to AWS. Crossplane's abstraction enables portability beyond compute/network/storage into databases and other services.

The AWS operator only targets AWS resources and can't move to minikube, Azure or elsewhere. Some would call that vendor lock-in, whereas Crossplane's idea is using services with apps that stay portable across cloud providers.

On Crossplane vs Terraform: you would likely use both. Terraform provisions the Kubernetes cluster and non-application infrastructure. Crossplane brings app-specific cloud infra (e.g., a MySQL DB) into the same config files as the Kubernetes app, instead of pre-provisioning with Terraform and keeping it in sync.

Skeptical take: 'Why do i need to configure a mysql database for a wordpress if that wordpress always needs a mysql database? While i really like the idea, i'm looking forward to see if we moved our problems down to the operator code or if those configuration problems are gone.'

'I really like idea of separating a service's infra requirements from it's infra implementation details.' The commenter questioned pitching the developer/administrator separation of concerns, though: 'How does this work in a world where developers administer their own services?'

GitLab's CEO said they were excited about Crossplane as 'the missing technology' to make multi-cloud convenient. Their Helm chart doesn't set up object storage or cloud-managed PostgreSQL/Redis, so they planned to deploy GitLab via Crossplane and later integrate it into Auto DevOps for app portability.

One commenter said they wouldn't trust a major cloud provider to give competitors equal footing with a package like Crossplane. They would prefer to trust the company behind the open source. They also observed that the names Crossplane and Upbound 'seem a little too unrelated.'
'Thanks for CrossPlane, this will work if you guys stay true to your mission. A frustrated cloud user.'

Asked whether it competes with Rancher 2.0, one commenter said it seems complementary. You would run Crossplane on a Rancher 2.0 cluster and get automatically provisioned databases, since it extends the default kube system and Rancher just provides an interface.

This commenter has often seen large teams deal with Terraform sprawl by splitting it into ever smaller modules (less drift blast radius, less visibility) or using '-target' applies. Terraform suits small teams, but Crossplane 'appears to have a clear yaml syntax (easy enough to commit to source control) and runs a control plane for enforcement (easier than setting up Atlantis, I imagine).'
'Really nice to see Crossplane and Upbound maturing!'
